newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary says years required to upgrade military.
newsitem.headline: Hungary says years required to upgrade military.

text.p: Hungary's defence minister warned U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen on Thursday it could take the young democracy 10 years to upgrade its Soviet-armed military to full NATO standards.

"We have to set our priorities right," Defence Minister Gyorgy Keleti said at a news conference with Cohen. He stressed that economic stability was the first goal for Hungary, invited this week to join the western alliance in 1999.

"I think that we need at least eight to 10 years for our military to be fully compatible with other armies of NATO," Keleti said, stressing that air defence and reorganising the Soviet-style army headed Budapest's military reform list.

Arguing that good radios and English-language training were more important initially than new fighter jets, Cohen told reporters he agreed with Budapest's careful budgeting approach to military change.
In a speech to Parliament he cautioned that certain basic NATO standards must be met, but praised Hungary's leaders for steps taken so far on financial and other reforms.
"We recognise that Hungary is ready to take the next steps to becoming a full (NATO) member and to accept all the rights and responsibilities of membership," he told lawmakers.
But he added that the alliance "must make sure NATO's strength is not diminished, only enhanced," in its expansion efforts.

Cohen, midway through a European trip that will also carry him to Ukraine and Bulgaria, visited later on Thursday with U.S. troops at the Taszar military base in Hungary. The base is a transit and supply point for Americans serving with a NATO- led peacekeeping force in Bosnia.

In Budapest, Keleti said Hungary was moving first to improve air defence with new radars and French anti-aircraft missiles and was putting a priority on training officers and lower ranks in western military standards.

Hungary has said that it is anxious to meet demands by NATO for military compatibility with western armies and will increase its defence budget from a current 1.8 per cent of gross domestic product to 2.2 per cent in the years ahead.
But despite plans for an eventual purchase of up to 30 new jet fighters for up to $1 billion, Keleti suggested that costly arms would take a back seat to military basics such as command and control.
"The economic stability of the Republic of Hungary is an important factor that will have to be taken into account," he said.

Cohen estimated it would cost a total of $27 billion to $35 billion over the next 13 years to include the three former Warsaw Pact countries in NATO, and that a third of that cost would be bourne by the three states themselves.
But Keleti said Hungary's costs would not necessarily be equal to those of Poland and the Czech Republic.
Cohen will begin a two-day visit to Ukraine on Friday and then visit the Bulgarian capital Sofia before flying home to Washington on Moday.
